Name: Improper Expiration of Cached Data
Description:
The product uses or supports data in a cache, but it does
	    not properly specify an expiration with a date, time, or
	    time period that is sufficient for the intended security
	    policy of the product or its adminstrators.

ModesOfIntroduction.Note: Developers might inadvertently omit specifying a specific expiration for the data. With some cache mechanisms, this could cause the data to be labeled as having no expiration at all.

CommonConsequences.Note: If the cached data is used for security-critical functionality such as authentication, authorization, or identity, then this might allow users or adversaries to perform operations beyond their expected lifetime. If the data is old but used for identification, such as DNS lookup results, then the stale data could point to entities that are no longer controlled by the intended owner.

PotentialMitigations.Description: For each type of cached data, determine the best lifetime that balances efficiency provided by the cache with the security implications of the data becoming too stale. Explicitly specify an expiration date or time period.

Entries.IntroText: Some JVM implementations cache DNS resolution results by default.

Entries.ExampleCode: The expiry setting of the cached results might either be inappropriately long for the program or set to never expire.

Entries.BodyText: This results in a situation where changes to DNS records seemingly do not take effect in the program. This could cause the product to communicate with IP addresses that are no longer associated with the updated DNS records.

Entries.ExampleCode: To mitigate this situation, the DNS cache setting networkaddress.cache.ttl for the JVM needs to be set appropriately.

ObservedExamples.Description: RESTful search engine caches DNS hostname lookups forever in order to prevent DNS spoofing attacks, but it will not be able to detect when the hostnames resolve to a different IP address.
